pool.prompt: A technician accidentally connects a yellow OS2 SMF patch cord to an aqua OM4 MMF patch panel port. What is the most likely result?
choices: The link works fine — both have 125 um cladding diameter so they're compatible
The link experiences massive signal loss (likely 20+ dB) because the 9 um SMF core doesn't fill the 50 um MMF core, so most light from the MMF misses the SMF core
The link works at reduced speed (downgrade from 10GbE to 1GbE)
The OM4 cable converts the 1310 nm SMF wavelength to 850 nm automatically
pool.explanation: The 9 um SMF core is far smaller than the 50 um MMF core. Light coming from the MMF spreads across the full 50 um, but only a tiny fraction falls within the 9 um SMF core, causing 20-30 dB of loss — effectively killing the link.
pool.fieldNote: Color is a helpful cue (yellow = SMF, aqua = OM3/OM4, lime = OM5, orange = OM1/OM2) but always read the print on the cable — don't trust jacket color alone.

pool.prompt: For a 12 km OSP fiber run connecting a rural OLT headend to a remote distribution hub, which fiber type is required?
choices: OM4 multimode — it supports higher bandwidth
OS2 single-mode (G.652.D) — 12 km is far beyond any MMF reach limit
OM5 multimode — it supports SWDM4 and can handle the distance
Either SMF or MMF — the distance is within OM3 spec
pool.explanation: OM3 MMF tops out at roughly 300 m for 10GbE at 850 nm; OM4 at roughly 400 m. No multimode fiber reaches beyond roughly 550 m for any standard Ethernet application. A 12 km run requires OS2 single-mode fiber.

pool.prompt: The OS1/OS2 fiber category designations under ISO/IEC 11801 map to which ITU-T G.652 sub-grades?
choices: OS1 = G.652.B/C; OS2 = G.652.D only
OS1 = G.652.A/B (max ~1.0 dB/km); OS2 = G.652.C/D (max ~0.4 dB/km, low/zero water-peak)
OS1 and OS2 both map to the same G.652 sub-grade, differing only in jacket color
OS1 = G.657; OS2 = G.652 — the two designations refer to entirely different ITU-T standard families
pool.explanation: OS1 corresponds to the older G.652.A/B specs (higher attenuation, max ~1.0 dB/km). OS2 corresponds to the low/zero water-peak G.652.C/D specs (max ~0.4 dB/km), which is what nearly all current OSP deployments specify.
pool.citation: ISO/IEC 11801 OS1/OS2 category mapping to ITU-T G.652 sub-grades.

pool.prompt: Why does OM3/OM4/OM5 fiber have a higher bandwidth rating than OM1/OM2, even though all are 50 um core multimode?
choices: OM3/OM4/OM5 uses a graded-index core profile optimized for 850 nm VCSEL launch conditions — this reduces modal dispersion by restricting which modes are excited
OM3/OM4/OM5 uses single-mode glass chemistry even though the core is larger
OM3/OM4/OM5 is manufactured at lower attenuation, which automatically increases bandwidth
OM3 was retroactively renamed from OM1 — it's the same fiber with a new label
pool.explanation: OM3/OM4/OM5 are 'laser-optimized' — their graded-index profile is tailored for 850 nm VCSEL sources, which excite fewer high-order modes than an LED overfilled launch. Fewer excited modes means less modal dispersion and more usable bandwidth at a given length.

pool.prompt: What is the primary reason a fiber optic crew must never assume compatibility between SMF and MMF connectors based on physical fit alone?
choices: SMF and MMF connectors use physically different connector housings that cannot be mated
SMF and MMF often use identical connector types (LC, SC) that will physically mate, but the drastically different core sizes cause severe optical loss — a physical fit does not imply an optical match
MMF connectors are always keyed to prevent mating with SMF connectors
SMF and MMF cannot both use the same wavelength, making mating irrelevant
pool.explanation: Connector housings (LC, SC, etc.) are standardized independent of the fiber type inside — an SMF LC connector will physically mate with an MMF LC adapter. The mismatch that matters is optical (core size), not mechanical, which is exactly why color-coding and jacket printing exist as a secondary safeguard.

pool.prompt: What effective modal bandwidth (EMB) test methodology distinguishes OM3+ multimode fiber testing from older OM1/OM2 testing?
choices: EMB testing evaluates fiber under laser (VCSEL-like) launch conditions rather than the older overfilled LED launch condition, since laser-optimized fiber's advantage only shows up under realistic laser launch
EMB testing is identical to overfilled launch bandwidth testing, just renamed
EMB testing only applies to single-mode fiber
EMB testing measures attenuation, not bandwidth, despite its name
pool.explanation: The effective modal bandwidth (EMB) metric was introduced specifically because laser-optimized (OM3+) fiber's performance advantage depends on realistic VCSEL-like launch conditions — an older overfilled-launch bandwidth test wouldn't reveal the improvement.
pool.citation: IEEE 802.3 effective modal bandwidth methodology; TIA-492AAAD.

pool.prompt: A designer must choose between SMF and MMF for a new intra-building data center run of 80 meters at 10GbE. What is the strongest argument for MMF (OM4) in this scenario?
choices: MMF always has lower attenuation than SMF at any distance
At this short distance, MMF transceivers (VCSEL-based) are typically lower-cost than SMF transceivers, and OM4's reach easily covers 80 m at 10GbE
SMF physically cannot operate over distances under 1 km
MMF is required by TIA-568 for all intra-building runs regardless of distance
pool.explanation: For short intra-building runs well within multimode's reach limits, MMF/VCSEL transceiver economics typically beat SMF/laser transceiver costs — SMF's long-reach advantage isn't needed at 80 m, so the cost argument favors MMF in this scenario.

pool.prompt: Match each fiber grade/color convention to its category.
pool.explanation: Jacket color is a helpful visual cue (yellow=SMF, aqua=OM3/OM4, lime=OM5, orange=OM1/OM2) but is a convention, not a guarantee — always confirm with the jacket print before mating connectors, since color conventions can vary by vendor or region.
